title: Cash Flow Problems: 7 Causes & How to Fix Them
summary: Find seven common causes of cash flow problems, from late invoices to excess inventory. Use a practical forecast and action checklist to plan your next steps.
body_markdown:
Updated November 26, 2026. Cover:[Allen Y / Unsplash](https://unsplash.com/photos/multiple-cash-registers-with-computer-monitors-at-a-checkout-counter-UaMMROu5fq0) . Illustrative photograph.


A profitable month can end with a difficult payroll week. Revenue on the income statement and money available in the bank move on different schedules.


**Cash flow problems** start when the timing or amount of cash coming in cannot comfortably cover the cash going out. Before looking for more funding, identify which part of the cycle is creating the pressure.


## What Causes Cash Flow Problems?


Some **cash flow issues** come from a temporary timing gap. Others reflect weak margins, shrinking demand or commitments the business can no longer support. Match the response to the cause.


The[Federal Reserve's 2026 employer-firm report release](https://www.clevelandfed.org/collections/press-releases/2026/pr-20260303-fed-survey-small-business-optimism-wanes-as-performance-metrics-hold-steady) identified rising costs as the leading financial challenge in its 2025 survey. Its findings describe surveyed businesses, not the probability that any particular business will run short.

## 1. Customers Pay Later Than Expected


A sale creates a receivable. It becomes spendable cash when payment clears. Incorrect invoices, missing purchase-order numbers and unresolved delivery disputes can all delay that point.


**What to do:** confirm billing requirements before shipping, invoice promptly and assign an owner to each dispute. Ask customers for specific payment dates. Use[accounts receivable management](https://www.dripcapital.com/en-us/resources/blog/accounts-receivable-management) controls alongside an aging report.


## 2. Too Much Cash Sits in Inventory


Buying ahead can protect supply, but excess stock also consumes cash before a sale occurs. Slow-moving products may need storage and discounting while faster-selling items still require replenishment.


**What to do:** separate fast sellers from aging stock, revise reorder quantities and stop repeating purchases purely because the unit discount looks attractive. The[inventory turnover guide](https://www.dripcapital.com/en-us/resources/blog/inventory-turnover-ratio) helps you check the overall pattern.


## 3. Sales Grow Faster Than Funding


A larger order can require more vendor payments, freight and labor before the customer pays. Growth can increase the cash needed to operate even when the order is profitable.


**What to do:** build an order-level cash timeline before accepting the commitment. Include deposits, shipment dates, customer terms and a late-payment scenario. Confirm that the business can fund the lowest projected balance.


### Find where the cash is held


**Unpaid invoices**


Check aging and disputed balances.


**Stock on shelves**


Review replenishment and slow movers.


**Low-margin orders**


Reprice or change the cost structure.


**Timing mismatch**


Map due dates against expected receipts.


## 4. Margins No Longer Cover Costs


Higher freight, labor or purchase costs can shrink the cash left from each sale. If pricing stays unchanged, more volume may increase workload without producing enough cash to support it.


**What to do:** recalculate the contribution from each product or customer after its direct costs. Review discounts, minimum order sizes and service commitments. Our[MOQ guide](https://www.dripcapital.com/en-us/resources/blog/moq-meaning) explains the purchasing side of that decision.

## 5. Fixed Bills Outlast the Busy Season


Rent, payroll, subscriptions and scheduled payments can continue while seasonal receipts fall. An annual profit forecast may conceal the weakest month.


**What to do:** map the low-season cash balance before making high-season commitments. Ask vendors about agreed timing changes early, and budget reserves for the months when collections slow. Review[Seasonal Business Loans](https://www.dripcapital.com/en-us/resources/blog/seasonal-business-loans) in the context of a complete seasonal plan.


## 6. Taxes and Debt Payments Arrive Together


Several manageable obligations can create a difficult week when their dates overlap. Principal repayments and asset purchases can reduce cash without appearing as matching current expenses on the income statement.


**What to do:** put actual payment dates into the forecast. Maintain a tax calendar with your accountant and check loan schedules. Negotiate changes before missing a commitment, and use agreed terms rather than assuming a payment can be delayed.


## 7. The Forecast Uses Hopeful Collection Dates


A forecast based on every customer paying exactly on time can look healthy until the first delay. Unconfirmed sales and expected refunds can add false comfort.


**What to do:** distinguish confirmed receipts from estimates, update the forecast weekly and compare the previous forecast with what actually happened. Record forecast differences.


## How to Fix Cash Flow Problems: Start With a Weekly View


A practical starting point is a rolling 13-week cash forecast. This is an operating recommendation, not a mandatory accounting standard. Record opening cash, expected receipts, planned payments and closing cash each week.


### A Simple Cash-Forecast Example


Suppose a week starts with $25,000, expected receipts are $40,000 and payments total $55,000. Closing cash would be $10,000. If $20,000 of those receipts slips into the following week, the same plan produces a $10,000 shortfall.


These illustrative numbers show why payment timing deserves its own review. A monthly sales total would not identify which bill becomes difficult to pay first.


### Weekly cash review cheat sheet


**Opening cash**


Use funds actually available.


**Receipts**


Separate confirmed dates from estimates.


**Payments**


Include taxes, principal and purchases.


**Downside**


Move a large receipt later and test the balance.


### Decide What Needs Action First


Prioritize essential operations and legal obligations with appropriate professional advice. Follow up on collectable invoices, investigate disputed balances and reconsider purchases that can be changed without breaking commitments. Then evaluate funding for a defined gap and repayment source.


**Negative cash flow** means cash outflows exceed inflows over the period being measured. It can accompany investment or growth, but repeated shortfalls need a clear explanation and a credible funding plan.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### Can a profitable business have cash flow problems?


Yes. Profit and cash reflect different timing and accounting effects. Unpaid invoices, inventory purchases and principal repayments can leave a profitable business short of cash.


### What is the first step in fixing cash flow issues?


Build a dated forecast of available cash, expected receipts and required payments. Then identify the invoices, purchases or obligations causing the earliest shortfall.


### Is negative cash flow always a sign of failure?


No. It can result from investment, seasonality or growth. Persistent shortfalls still need an explanation, a funding source and a realistic path to sufficient cash.


### Will a loan solve cash flow problems?


A loan can help fund a defined timing gap if repayment is affordable. It also adds payments, so weak margins or repeated collection failures still need attention.


### How often should I update a cash forecast?


A weekly update is a useful starting point for an active business. Review it more frequently when cash is tight or a large payment changes timing.
